current.text: Round 6: Argon picked C. C starts spilling out of the drain about 20s too late (5:12 vs 4:52 in REAL) and stays flooded way too long, REAL drains off the floor by 10:32 while C remains flooded past 17:32.

moments.evidence: Water spills out of the drain in REAL and B, while A and C are still inside the drain.
Water spread in REAL matches A best; B has spread too far, and C has barely spilled over.
In REAL, the water is draining back and the drain rim becomes visible, but all simulations remain completely submerged. C has the lowest depth (foreground cables stay unsubmerged longest).
In REAL, the floor has drained and water is receding into the drain pit, whereas A, B, and C still have the entire floor deeply flooded.
At the end of the clip, C begins to drain enough to expose the foreground cables, whereas A and B remain deeper.

log.text: Three Managed Agents test three theories of how water enters the basement.

door.report: We tested the baseline parameters and then reduced outlet_cd and p3_roughness to maximize surcharge into s4 over the door weir while varying p7_diameter_m, which had little effect on the basement because r5 is closed at a 99 m offset. While the dry check passed with 0.0 mm peak basement depth and continuity errors stayed below 5% at the best knobs (outlet_cd = 0.18, p7_diameter_m = 0.05, p3_roughness = 0.009), the calibration landmarks failed to fit within 60 s (wet onset at 360 s vs. 269 s target, peak at 630 s vs. 474 s target) and the basement never receded because water spilled over the 40 mm door crest remains trapped in s6 with r5 closed. Consequently, the door hypothesis looks very weak and cannot explain the observed basement flooding and recession dynamics.
